title: Operating Lease Subsequent Accounting
description: Understand single lease expense and subsequent measurement for operating leases.
html:
Operating leases

Operating leases also generally result in recognition of a right-of-use asset and lease liability by the lessee.

However, their subsequent expense recognition differs from finance leases.

Single lease cost

For an operating lease, the lessee generally recognizes a single lease cost, typically on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

Simple example

Assume an operating lease requires total fixed payments of $60,000 over five years, with no other adjustments affecting this simple example.

$60,000 ÷ 5 years = $12,000 annual lease cost

The lease liability still uses interest

The lease liability itself continues to be measured using an interest-based roll-forward.

Interest = Beginning Lease Liability × Periodic Discount Rate
Ending Lease Liability = Beginning Liability + Interest − Payment

Example

Beginning lease liability: $40,000

Discount rate: 5%

Year-end payment: $10,000

Interest on liability

$40,000 × 5% = $2,000

Ending lease liability

$40,000 + $2,000 − $10,000 = $32,000

What makes operating accounting different?

Although interest is used in measuring the lease liability, the operating lease generally presents a single lease cost.

The change in the ROU asset is therefore determined in a way that produces the required single lease-cost pattern.

Do not confuse these

Finance lease: interest and ROU asset amortization are recognized separately.

Operating lease: generally produces a single lease cost.

Big picture

Finance

Interest expense

+

ROU asset amortization

Operating

Generally a single lease cost over the lease term

quiz.prompt: An operating lease liability begins the year at $60,000. The annual discount rate is 5%, and the year-end payment is $14,000. What is the ending lease liability?
